common_name: Spring Frost Distylium (Variegated White-and-Green New-Growth Evergreen Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, average garden soil in full sun to partial shade; give Spring Frost a spot where its pale emerging foliage is visible up close, since the variegation is its main seasonal draw rather than bloom.

directions: Spring Frost is a patented distylium selection whose new leaves emerge creamy white with scattered green flecking and a thin rose-red edge, maturing to green with a lighter margin that keeps the shrub looking frost-dusted through each flush of growth. Like other distylium it bears small, petal-less, maroon late-winter flowers with prominent red stamens that pass largely unnoticed against the showier foliage display. Give it morning sun or filtered light through the day, since deep shade mutes the variegation contrast while harsh afternoon sun in hot climates can scorch the lighter leaf tissue. It otherwise shares the genus's tolerance for average to wet soil and resistance to deer, scale, and leaf spot, needing only an occasional light shaping to keep its rounded habit tidy.
sources: Southern Plant Group (U.S. Plant Patent PP25,833)

common_name: Bronze Beauty Ternstroemia (Bronze New-Growth Southern Cleyera)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade, giving afternoon shade protection in the hottest zones; Bronze Beauty grows quickly into a sizable screening shrub, so allow room for its eventual height.

directions: Bronze Beauty is a long-grown, patented ternstroemia selection whose glossy green foliage emerges a vivid bronzy-red continuously through the growing season, giving the plant near-constant color contrast rather than a single spring flush. It grows a notable two to three feet per year toward its mature height, making it one of the faster, larger ternstroemia cultivars and a dependable choice for privacy screens, informal hedges, or tall background plantings rather than small foundation beds. Fragrant creamy flowers in late spring are followed by small red berries, and the shrub tolerates full sun, partial shade, or full shade alike, though afternoon shade reduces leaf scorch risk in the hottest parts of its range. It adapts to most well-drained soils including clay, resists deer browsing, and needs only periodic shaping to control its vigorous growth rather than any routine disease or pest management.

common_name: Tricolor Cleyera (Yellow-and-Green Variegated Japanese Cleyera, Hosaba Fukurin)

planting.note: Plant container specimens in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; reserve full sun for mild coastal climates only, since direct afternoon sun elsewhere scorches the lighter leaf markings.

directions: Tricolor Cleyera, also sold as 'Variegata' or 'Hosaba Fukurin', is a slow-growing variegated selection of Japanese cleyera marked by gray-green marbled centers edged in yellow, with a red flush that intensifies through the colder months. Like the species it produces small, fragrant, cream-colored flowers in late spring followed by dark berries, set against dense, leathery evergreen foliage carried on an upright frame. Grow it in partial to full shade, since the variegated leaf tissue burns more readily in direct sun than solid-green cleyera, and provide shelter from drying winter winds at the colder end of its range. It makes an effective brightening accent among darker camellias, azaleas, or hollies in a shaded border, growing slowly enough that it rarely needs more than occasional light pruning to keep its naturally neat form.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

common_name: Ki Midori Nakafu Daphniphyllum (Gold-Centered Variegated Yuzuriha)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun, which can scorch the pale leaf centers; remove any branches that revert to solid green promptly, since they grow faster and will overtake the variegated wood if left unchecked.

directions: Ki Midori Nakafu is a rare, highly sought variegated selection of the Japanese evergreen Daphniphyllum macropodum, with large, leathery, rhododendron-like leaves marked by a bright chartreuse-to-gold center surrounded by a darker green margin. Like the species it carries its new leaves on distinctive red-tinged petioles and holds inconspicuous spring flowers followed by small blue-black fruit on female plants, but its chief appeal is purely foliar. Because variegated shoots grow more slowly than plain green reversions, prune out any solid-green branches as soon as they appear to keep the variegation from being crowded out over time. Give it humus-rich, evenly moist soil and partial shade, since strong direct sun can scorch the lightly pigmented leaf centers more readily than on the green-leaved species, and expect a slow-to-moderate pace toward its eventual size as a substantial shaded specimen or accent shrub.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade with shelter from cold winter wind; Variegatum is noticeably less cold-hardy than plain-leaved Daphniphyllum macropodum, so site it in a protected spot toward the warmer end of its range.

directions: Variegatum is an exceedingly rare, long-grown variegated form of the Japanese evergreen Daphniphyllum macropodum, bearing broad, irregular creamy-white margins around a dark green leaf center, with the pale edge occasionally reaching nearly to the midrib on individual leaves. It shares the species' coarse-textured, leathery, rhododendron-like foliage on red-tinged petioles and inconspicuous spring flowers followed by dark fruit on female plants, but grows more slowly and tolerates less cold than the green-leaved type, making winter wind protection and a sheltered, shaded site important for success outside the mildest parts of its range. Watch for and remove any shoots that revert to solid green, since they outgrow the variegated wood and will gradually overwhelm the cultivar's ornamental pattern if left unpruned. Use it as a protected specimen in a shaded courtyard or woodland garden rather than an exposed foundation planting.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)
